'''Carina Curto''' (born 15 April 1978) is an American [[mathematician]], a professor at [[Pennsylvania State University]], and a [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Sloan Research Fellow]].<ref name=":200">{{Cite news|url=https://www.math.unl.edu/newsletter/data/2011Department_of_Mathematics_Newsletter.pdf|title=UNL Math News - Winter 2011|work=Math News|access-date=2018-08-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sites.psu.edu/mathbio/faculty/|title=Faculty {{!}} Mathematical Biology at Penn State|website=sites.psu.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2018-07-31}}</ref> She is known for her work on mathematical [[neuroscience]], including the applications of mathematics in both theoretical and [[computational neuroscience]]. Her recent work is funded by the [[BRAIN Initiative]].<ref name="quanta2018">{{Cite news|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematician-carina-curto-thinks-like-a-physicist-to-solve-neuroscience-problems-20180619/|title=Mathematician Carina Curto Thinks Like a Physicist to Solve Neuroscience Problems {{!}} Quanta Magazine|work=Quanta Magazine|access-date=2018-07-31}}</ref> She is an associate editor at SIAGA, a [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] journal on applied [[algebra]] and [[geometry]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.personal.psu.edu/cpc16/|title=Carina's website|website=www.personal.psu.edu|access-date=2018-07-31}}</ref> and on the editorial board at [[Physical Review|Physical Review Research]].<ref name="PhysicsRev">{{Cite web|url=https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/staff/|title=Physical Review Research website|access-date=2021-05-03}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Curto was born to [[Argentines|Argentine]] parents and grew up in [[Iowa City, Iowa|Iowa City]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://physicsoflivingsystems.org/brainstructureandfunction/bios/|title=Bios|date=2013-05-03|work=Physical and Mathematical Principles of Brain Structure and Function|access-date=2018-08-15|language=en-US}}</ref> She attended [[Iowa City West High School]]. During her school years, she attended courses at the [[University of Iowa]], including advanced [[mathematics]] classes, [[physics]], [[computer science]], [[French literature]], and more.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|date=March 2018|title=In Honor of Women's History Month |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201803/201803FullIssue.pdf|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|volume=65}}</ref> In 1996, she began studying for an [[A.B. degree|A.B]]. in [[Physics]] at [[Harvard University]]. During her time at Harvard, she was awarded prizes including the Detur Book Prize, one of Harvard's oldest awards, and the [[American Physical Society]] minority scholarship.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/minorities/honors/scholarship/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Curto&first_nm=Carina&year=1997|title=Prize Recipient|website=www.aps.org|language=en|access-date=2018-08-31}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/206746689/|title=Iowa City Press-Citizen, Friday, January 16, 1998|date=1998-01-16|work=Iowa City Press-Citizen|access-date=2018-08-31}}</ref> After graduating from Harvard in 2000 and being awarded the [[NSF-GRF|NSF Graduate Research Fellowship]], Curto started a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D]] in mathematics at [[Duke University]]. Curto's Ph.D. focused on mathematical [[string theory]] and [[algebraic geometry]].<ref name=":0" /> Her thesis was titled 'Matrix Model Superpotentials and [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi-Yau Spaces]]: an ADE Classification'.<ref name=":201" />

== Career and research ==
Once Curto gained her Ph.D., she moved to [[Rutgers University]] in [[New Jersey]], working as a postdoctoral associate in a neuroscience lab at the Center for Molecular and Behavioral Neuroscience.<ref name="quanta2018" /> After three years at Rutgers, she returned to working in mathematics, focusing on neuroscience from a more mathematical perspective, and moved to the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences|Courant Institute of Mathematics]] at [[New York University]], then to the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|University of Nebraska-Lincoln]], followed by the [[Pennsylvania State University]], and now [[Brown University]], where she is Professor of Applied Mathematics and Brain Science in the Division of Applied Mathematics and the Carney Institute for Brain Science.{{Cite web|url=https://ccurto.github.io|title=Personal Website|access-date=2026-09-08}}

=== Network connectivity ===
Her research focuses on the interplay between the connectivity and dynamics of the [[brain]] and involves studying neural recordings and analysing the patterns of the activities. This network analysis aims to understand the connections between the [[neuron]]s and their patterns.<ref name="quanta2018" /> Traditionally, neuroscientists rely on tools from [[physics]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://neurosciencenews.com/math-method-neural-activity-2912/|title=New Math Method Reveals Structure of Neural Activity|date=2015-10-20|work=Neuroscience News|access-date=2018-09-06|language=en-US}}</ref> But Curto's approach uses tools from pure mathematics, particularly [[algebraic geometry]], which is applied to the activity data of the neurons. Curto's research is significant in the field of [[connectomics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2018/04/02/cross-pollination-at-cosyne-2018/|title=Cross-Pollination at Cosyne 2018 {{!}} Simons Foundation|website=www.simonsfoundation.org|language=en-US|access-date=2018-09-06|date=2018-04-02}}</ref> For instance, one study showed how neural activities can drastically change by slightly changing the structure of the networks, which has implications for the study of brain disorders such as [[Parkinson's disease]] and [[schizophrenia]].<ref name=":200" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2018/05/03/simple-networks-generate-complex-dynamics/|title=Simple Networks Generate Complex Dynamics {{!}} Simons Foundation|website=www.simonsfoundation.org|language=en-US|access-date=2018-09-06|date=2018-05-03}}</ref>

Along with Katherine Morrison from the [[University of Northern Colorado]], and with funding from the government's BRAIN Initiative grant and the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]], Curto is working on Combinatorial Threshold-Linear Networks, CTLNs. These models enable the observations of emergent patterns, such as neuronal sequences and complex rhythms, and can also be used to predict features of the dynamics, something that has been seemingly difficult to predict.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Morrison|first1=Katherine|last2=Curto|first2=Carina|date=2018-04-04|title=Predicting neural network dynamics via graphical analysis|eprint=1804.01487|class=q-bio.NC}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.brown.edu/academics/applied-mathematics/graphs-neural-networks-and-emergent-dynamics-brain|title=Graphs, neural networks, and emergent dynamics in the brain {{!}} Division of Applied Mathematics|website=www.brown.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-03}}</ref>

Aligned with her research, Curto, alongside Morrison, also created a project called Network Songs, which originally started out as a gimmick. This is a collection of songs, that show the rhythmic activity of the networks. The basis of the songs were created by assigning a note on the piano to each neuron. Curto explains that sometimes certain patterns are better distinguished by the ear, than by the eye, hence the purpose of this particular representation of the network data.<ref name="quanta2018" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://slideplayer.com/slide/9703374/|title=NETWORK SONGS !! created by Carina Curto & Katherine Morrison January 2016 Input: a simple directed graph G satisfying two rules: 1. G is an oriented. - ppt download|website=slideplayer.com|access-date=2018-09-03}}</ref>

== Awards and personal life ==
Curto has been the recipient of numerous grants and awards, including becoming a [[Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship Foundation|Woodrow Wilson National Fellow]] and an [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Alfred Sloan Research Fellow]]. Additionally, in 2012, Curto was named a [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|UNL]] Academic Star.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.unl.edu/department/awards/faculty|title=Faculty Awards {{!}} Department of Mathematics {{!}} Nebraska|last=Network|first=University of Nebraska-Lincoln {{!}} Web Developer|website=www.math.unl.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-03}}</ref> In 2021 she was named a Simons Fellow in Mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-02-04|title=2021 Simons Fellows in Mathematics and Theoretical Physics Announced|url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2021/02/04/2021-simons-fellows-in-mathematics-and-theoretical-physics-announced/|access-date=2021-07-18|website=Simons Foundation|language=en-US}}</ref>

In March 2018, the [[American Mathematical Society]], AMS, included Curto in a list of 27 female mathematicians in honour of [[Women's History Month]], publishing a profile of her in the [[Notices of the American Mathematical Society|AMS Notices journal]].<ref name=":2" />

Throughout her years as a mathematician, Curto has taken part in many events and boards to promote women in mathematics. This includes being involved with the Women In Math club at [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|UNL]] and being part of the Nebraska Conference for Undergraduate Women in Mathematics, NCUWM, organizing committee.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.unl.edu/math-club/events/archive|title=Math Club Events Archive {{!}} Department of Mathematics {{!}} Nebraska|last=Network|first=University of Nebraska-Lincoln {{!}} Web Developer|website=www.math.unl.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.math.unl.edu/~ncuwm/16thAnnual/ncuwm_aboutus.php|title=Nebraska Conference for Undergraduate Women in Mathematics {{!}} About Us|last=Network|first=University of Nebraska-Lincoln {{!}} Web Developer|website=www.math.unl.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-06}}</ref>

Curto is also an amateur [[tennis]] player. In 1995, when at high school, she became the Double State Champion.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iowacityschools.org/site/handlers/filedownload.ashx?moduleinstanceid=28282&dataid=38664&FileName=State%20Championships.pdf|title=Trojan Hall of Fame - Iowa City Schools|date=2018-05-24|access-date=2018-09-04}}</ref> Furthermore, in 1996-1997 she was the Varsity Letter Winner for Women's tennis at Harvard.
